symptoms: Elevated body temperature, chills, shivering, sweating, headache, and general malaise.
indication: Symptomatic relief of mild-to-moderate pyrexia (fever) in adults and children.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 2.1 (Non-opioids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines)
safety_note: Do not exceed maximum daily limit (4g/24h in adults) to avoid severe liver toxicity. Avoid combining with other paracetamol-containing products. If fever persists over 3 days, consult a physician.

dosage_by_age.children: Weight-based dosing: 10–15 mg/kg per dose every 4–6 hours as needed; maximum 4 doses (60 mg/kg) in 24 hours. Always use calibrated pediatric oral measuring syringe or cup with oral suspension (120 mg/5 mL or 250 mg/5 mL). Never administer adult tablets to young infants without explicit pediatric calculation.
dosage_by_age.adults: 500 mg to 1,000 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed for fever or pain. Minimum dosing interval: 4 hours. Do not exceed 4,000 mg (4 g) in any 24-hour window.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dosing (500–1,000 mg every 4–6 hours). In frail elderly individuals, low body weight (<50 kg), or mild hepatic/renal compromise, a conservative ceiling of 2,000–3,000 mg/24h is recommended.

max_recommended_dose: 4,000 mg (4 g) per 24 hours for adults; 60 mg/kg/day for pediatric patients (not to exceed adult maximum).
side_effects: Rare at therapeutic doses: nausea, pruritus, allergic skin rash
Very rare: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, neutropenia
Overdose / Toxic ingestions: severe acute hepatic necrosis, acute liver failure, renal tubular necrosis
precautions_contraindications: Strictly contraindicated in severe active hepatic failure or acute liver disease. Caution in chronic alcohol dependence, severe renal impairment, chronic malnutrition, and G6PD deficiency. Critical Warning: Avoid combining with other paracetamol-containing combination medicines (e.g., OTC cold/cough syrups) to prevent accidental hepatotoxic overdose.
clinical_warning: Dosage depends on age, weight, formulation, liver health, kidney function, and other concurrent medicines. Do not self-medicate or exceed the stated dose. Consult a licensed healthcare provider.

indication: First-line management of mild non-inflammatory somatic and musculoskeletal pain.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 2.1
safety_note: Ensure proper dose interval (at least 4-6 hours apart). Patients with chronic liver impairment or chronic alcohol dependence should consult a doctor before use.

who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 2.1

symptoms: Localized swelling, warmth, joint stiffness, throbbing pain, soft tissue tenderness or sprains.
indication: Relief of pain and inflammation in musculoskeletal disorders, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and acute trauma.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 2.1
safety_note: Take with or after food to minimize gastrointestinal discomfort. Caution in patients with peptic ulcers, renal impairment, heart failure, or uncontrolled hypertension. Professional medical guidance recommended for prolonged courses.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 2.1.3, 5.2.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Inflammatory pain and joint stiffness in rheumatoid arthritis & osteoarthritis
Acute soft tissue injuries, sprains, strains, and dental inflammation
Acute mild-to-moderate migraine attack abortion
Fever in children when paracetamol is insufficient

dosage_by_age.children: Pediatric suspension (100 mg/5 mL): 5–10 mg/kg per dose orally every 6–8 hours as needed; maximum 30–40 mg/kg/day. Not recommended in infants under 3 months or weighing less than 5 kg without specialist supervision.
dosage_by_age.adults: 200 mg to 400 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed with or after food. Under medical supervision for inflammatory disorders: 400–600 mg every 6–8 hours.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. Elderly patients are at significantly higher risk for gastrointestinal ulceration/bleeding and renal hemodynamic compromise.

max_recommended_dose: 1,200 mg/24h for OTC self-care; up to 2,400 mg/24h under direct physician supervision.
side_effects: Dyspepsia, heartburn, epigastric discomfort, nausea
Gastrointestinal ulceration, occult bleeding, fluid retention
Hypertension exacerbation, elevated serum creatinine, headache
precautions_contraindications: Contraindicated in active peptic ulcer, severe heart failure (NYHA Class IV), advanced renal impairment, and history of aspirin/NSAID-induced asthma. Always administer with food or milk to minimize gastric mucosal irritation.
clinical_warning: Dosage depends on age, weight, cardiovascular risk, and gastrointestinal history. Do not use continuously without clinical review.

symptoms: Unilateral pulsating or throbbing head pain, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, visual aura.
indication: Acute symptomatic abortive therapy for mild-to-moderate migraine attacks.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 7.1 (Medicines for acute migraine attacks)
safety_note: Take early at migraine onset. Avoid long-term continuous use without medical supervision. If migraines occur frequently (>4 days/month), consult a neurologist for preventive therapy.

dosage_by_age.adults: 200 mg to 400 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed with or after food. Under medical supervision for inflammatory disorders: 400–600 mg every 6–8 hours.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. Elderly patients are at significantly higher risk for gastrointestinal ulceration/bleeding and renal hemodynamic compromise.

symptoms: Intense, agonizing pain from major surgery, severe trauma, advanced malignancies, or refractory acute injury.
indication: Management of moderate-to-severe acute pain and severe chronic cancer/palliative pain.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 2.2 (Opioid analgesics)
safety_note: STRICT MEDICAL SUPERVISION REQUIRED. High risk of dependence, respiratory depression, constipation, and sedation. Strictly strictly prohibited without direct registered specialist prescription and monitoring.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 1.3.4, 2.2.2, 7.4.13 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Severe acute somatic and visceral pain (major trauma, surgical procedures, myocardial infarction)
Chronic cancer pain and advanced palliative end-of-life care
Acute pulmonary edema adjunct in intensive care

dosage_by_age.children: Strictly administered under specialist pediatric hospital inpatient protocol (0.1–0.2 mg/kg per dose orally or IV) with continuous pulse oximetry and respiratory monitoring.
dosage_by_age.adults: Immediate-release oral: 5–10 mg every 4 hours initially for opioid-naive patients, titrated individually by palliative or pain specialists; IV: 2–5 mg slow titration.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Require lower starting doses (e.g. 2.5–5 mg) and longer dosing intervals due to reduced renal excretion, high sensitivity to central sedation, and fall risk.

max_recommended_dose: No arbitrary ceiling for opioid-tolerant cancer pain; strictly titrated against pain severity and respiratory rate under continuous medical supervision.
side_effects: Drowsiness, sedation, dizziness, confusion
Constipation (nearly universal; requires co-prescribed laxatives), nausea, vomiting
Respiratory depression, hypotension, physical dependence, tolerance
precautions_contraindications: Strictly contraindicated in acute severe respiratory depression, paralytic ileus, severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and head injury with raised intracranial pressure. Strictly controlled narcotic formulation (Schedule X / NDPS).
clinical_warning: STRICT MEDICAL SUPERVISION REQUIRED. High risk of dependence and life-threatening respiratory depression. Strictly prohibited without verified specialist prescription.

symptoms: Heartburn, retrosternal burning sensation, acid regurgitation, sour taste, epigastric discomfort after meals.
indication: Suppression of gastric acid secretion for symptomatic relief and mucosal healing in gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 17.1 (Anti-ulcer medicines)
safety_note: Best taken 30-60 minutes before breakfast. Long-term unmonitored use may impair vitamin B12, magnesium, and calcium absorption. Consult a physician for persistent symptoms or 'red flag' dysphagia.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 17.1.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and erosive esophagitis
Treatment and prophylaxis of gastric and duodenal peptic ulcers
Eradication of Helicobacter pylori (triple therapy regimens)
Prophylaxis of NSAID-induced gastric ulceration

dosage_by_age.children: Pediatric GERD / erosive esophagitis: 0.7–1.4 mg/kg once daily (10–20 mg) under pediatric specialist supervision.
dosage_by_age.adults: 20 mg to 40 mg once daily taken 30–60 minutes before morning breakfast. H. pylori eradication: 20 mg twice daily with antibiotics for 14 days.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose of 20 mg once daily. Long-term unmonitored use requires monitoring of bone density, magnesium, and vitamin B12.

max_recommended_dose: 40 mg/day for standard GERD/ulcer therapy; up to 80–120 mg/day in hypersecretory conditions (Zollinger-Ellison).
side_effects: Headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, flatulence
Long-term use: hypomagnesemia, Vitamin B12 deficiency, increased risk of Clostridioides difficile enteritis
precautions_contraindications: Exclude gastric malignancy before initiating long-term therapy as omeprazole may mask symptoms. Potential interaction with clopidogrel (CYP2C19 inhibition). Swallow capsules whole; do not crush.
clinical_warning: Do not use continuously for prolonged periods without medical evaluation of persistent heartburn or dysphagia.

symptoms: Burning epigastric pain (worse on empty stomach or nocturnal), bloating, early satiety, nausea, indigestion.
indication: Treatment and prophylaxis of gastric and duodenal ulcers, NSAID-associated ulceration, and H. pylori eradication regimens.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 17.1
safety_note: Prescription-guided full clinical course is essential for ulcer healing. If dark tarry stools, coffee-ground vomiting, or severe unexplained weight loss occur, seek immediate emergency endoscopy.

symptoms: Persistent urge to vomit, retching, acute post-operative emesis, or chemotherapy/radiation-induced emesis.
indication: Prevention and treatment of cytotoxic chemotherapy-induced, radiotherapy-induced, and postoperative nausea and vomiting.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 17.2 (Antiemetic medicines)

nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 7.4.14, 17.2.3 • Healthcare Level: S, T
common_uses: Prevention and management of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV)
Prevention and treatment of post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV)
Radiotherapy-induced emesis

dosage_by_age.adults: 4 mg to 8 mg orally every 8 hours as needed. Pre-chemotherapy: 8 mg to 16 mg IV/oral prior to treatment.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dosage. In hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C): maximum daily dose is 8 mg.

max_recommended_dose: 16 mg per single IV dose; 24 mg per day orally in divided doses.
side_effects: Headache, constipation, sensation of warmth or flushing
Transient asymptomatic ECG changes (dose-dependent QT prolongation)
precautions_contraindications: Contraindicated in congenital long QT syndrome. Caution with concurrent QT-prolonging medicines or electrolyte imbalances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia). Maximum 8 mg/day in severe hepatic impairment.
clinical_warning: Dose must be determined by clinical condition and route of administration. Monitor cardiac status in high-risk patients.

symptoms: Feeling sick, gastric fullness, delayed stomach emptying, nausea accompanied by abdominal distension or migraine.
indication: Symptomatic control of nausea, vomiting, and impaired gastrointestinal motility.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 17.2
safety_note: Use with caution due to risk of extrapyramidal reactions (acute dystonia), especially in children and young adults. Limit treatment duration as advised by a doctor. Contraindicated in gastrointestinal hemorrhage or bowel obstruction.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 7.4.10, 17.2.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Nausea and vomiting induced by migraine or gastrointestinal motility disorders
Diabetic gastroparesis and delayed gastric emptying
Gastrointestinal radiological transit facilitator

dosage_by_age.children: Contraindicated in infants under 1 year. Children 1–18 years: 0.1 to 0.15 mg/kg body weight per dose, maximum 3 times daily. Secondary option only due to neurological risks.
dosage_by_age.adults: 10 mg orally or IV/IM up to 3 times daily. Maximum recommended treatment duration is 5 consecutive days.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Dose reduction recommended due to high risk of extrapyramidal symptoms, parkinsonism, and irreversible tardive dyskinesia.

max_recommended_dose: 30 mg per 24 hours (or 0.5 mg/kg/day).
side_effects: Drowsiness, restlessness, lassitude
Extrapyramidal reactions (acute dystonia, oculogyric crisis, facial spasm)
Tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use, hyperprolactinemia
precautions_contraindications: Contraindicated in gastrointestinal hemorrhage, mechanical obstruction, perforation, and pheochromocytoma. Strictly avoid long-term therapy (>5 days).
clinical_warning: Risk of neurological movement disorders. Must be used at lowest effective dose for no more than 5 days.

symptoms: Frequent watery loose stools, thirst, dry mouth, decreased urine output, sunken eyes, fatigue, weakness.
indication: First-line therapy for prevention and correction of mild-to-moderate dehydration due to acute diarrhoea in all age groups.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 17.5.1 (Oral rehydration therapy)
safety_note: Dissolve the standard sachet precisely in the specified volume of clean drinking water (usually 1 litre). Do not boil prepared solution or add excess sugar. If vomiting prevents oral intake or severe dehydration signs develop, seek immediate intravenous care.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 17.6.1, 25.1.3 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
strengths_available: Powder for Solution: WHO Formulation (NaCl 2.6g, Dextrose 13.5g, KCl 1.5g, Trisodium Citrate 2.9g per liter)
common_uses: Prevention and treatment of acute dehydration from viral/bacterial diarrhea
Replacement of electrolyte and fluid losses in cholera and gastroenteritis

dosage_by_age.children: Children <2 years: 50–100 mL after each loose stool. Children 2–10 years: 100–200 mL after each loose stool. Continue normal feeding and breast milk.
dosage_by_age.adults: 200–400 mL after each loose stool, or ad libitum (2 to 3 liters/day based on thirst and ongoing fluid losses).
dosage_by_age.elderly: Administer in frequent small sips. Monitor carefully in patients with heart failure or chronic kidney disease to prevent fluid overload.

max_recommended_dose: Titrated to match fluid and electrolyte deficit; no arbitrary maximum, but adjust in renal compromise.
side_effects: Vomiting if consumed too rapidly (pause 10 minutes, then resume in sips)
Hypernatremia if incorrectly dissolved in insufficient water
precautions_contraindications: CRITICAL: Reconstitute strictly in exactly 1 Liter of clean drinking water. Do not mix with milk, juice, or additional sugar. Severe shock or unconsciousness requires IV fluids.
clinical_warning: Preparation volume accuracy is essential. Seek emergency care if child cannot drink, is lethargic, or has sunken eyes.

symptoms: Excessive thirst, dry mucous membranes, light-headedness, lethargy, dark concentrated urine from heat exhaustion or illness.
indication: Restoration of essential water, sodium, potassium, and chloride balance in fluid depletion states.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 17.5.1
safety_note: Administer small frequent sips. Ensure clean potable water is used for dilution. Patients with severe renal failure or heart failure require clinician monitoring of electrolyte loads.

symptoms: Infrequent bowel movements (<3 per week), hard lumpy stools, straining, sensation of incomplete rectal evacuation.
indication: Management of chronic and acute constipation; also used in hepatic encephalopathy.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 17.4 (Laxatives)
safety_note: May take 24 to 48 hours to produce clinical effect. Initial abdominal flatulence or cramping may occur. Maintain adequate dietary fluid and fiber intake. Seek medical evaluation for abrupt change in bowel habits.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 7.4.8, 17.5.3 • Healthcare Level: S, T
common_uses: Chronic functional and opioid-induced constipation
Hepatic encephalopathy treatment and prevention (ammonia reduction)

dosage_by_age.children: 1 month–1 year: 2.5 mL twice daily; 1–6 years: 5 mL twice daily; 7–14 years: 10 mL twice daily.
dosage_by_age.adults: Constipation: 15–30 mL once or twice daily. Hepatic encephalopathy: 30–50 mL 3 times daily titrated to produce 2–3 soft stools/day.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose (15–30 mL daily). Ensure adequate hydration to prevent dehydration.

max_recommended_dose: 45 mL/day for constipation; 90–150 mL/day for hepatic encephalopathy.
side_effects: Abdominal distension, flatulence, cramping, nausea, diarrhea with excessive dose
precautions_contraindications: Contraindicated in galactosemia and intestinal obstruction. Caution in diabetics (contains free galactose and lactose).
clinical_warning: May take 24–48 hours to produce laxative effect. Maintain adequate daily fluid intake.

symptoms: Abdominal discomfort, perianal pruritus (itching), visible worms in stool, unexplained weight loss, poor appetite.
indication: Eradication of intestinal roundworms (Ascaris), hookworms, pinworms, whipworms, and systemic helminthic infections.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.1.1 (Intestinal anthelmintics)
safety_note: Contraindicated during pregnancy (first trimester in particular). Medical supervision needed for systemic tissue helminthiasis. Ensure family members or close contacts are treated when indicated.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.1.1.1, 6.1.2.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Intestinal nematode infections (Ascaris lumbricoides, Enterobius, hookworm)
Neurocysticercosis and Echinococcus hydatid cyst disease

dosage_by_age.children: Children 1–2 years: 200 mg single dose. Children >2 years: 400 mg single dose. Not recommended in infants under 1 year.
dosage_by_age.adults: 400 mg as a single oral dose for intestinal worms; repeat in 2 weeks for enterobiasis. Hydatid disease: 400 mg twice daily for 28-day cycles with food.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose for intestinal deworming. Monitor hepatic enzymes during prolonged tissue therapy.

max_recommended_dose: 400 mg single dose for deworming; 800 mg/day divided for systemic tissue parasitic infections.
side_effects: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache
Reversible elevation of hepatic enzymes; leukopenia with prolonged high-dose therapy
precautions_contraindications: STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY (teratogenic in 1st trimester). Take with fatty meal to enhance absorption when treating systemic parasites.
clinical_warning: Verify pregnancy status before administration in women of childbearing potential. Repeat deworming after 14 days if recommended.

symptoms: Red annular scaly rash with raised edges, intense itching, maceration between toes (athlete's foot), groin rash (jock itch).
indication: Topical treatment of cutaneous dermatophytoses (tinea pedis, cruris, corporis), pityriasis versicolor, and cutaneous candidiasis.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 13.1 (Antifungal medicines - Topical)
safety_note: Apply thinly to clean, dry skin. Continue application for 1-2 weeks after visible lesions clear to prevent recurrence. Avoid contact with eyes. Discontinue if localized severe irritation or contact dermatitis occurs.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.5.2, 6.7.5.4, 11.1.1, 16.3 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Dermatophytosis (Tinea pedis / athlete's foot, Tinea cruris / jock itch, Tinea corporis)
Cutaneous candidiasis and candidal diaper rash
Vulvovaginal candidiasis (yeast infection)
Otomycosis (fungal ear infections)

dosage_by_age.children: Topical cream 1%: apply thinly to affected area 2 times daily for children >2 years under adult supervision.
dosage_by_age.adults: Topical: apply 2–3 times daily for 2–4 weeks. Vaginal pessary: 100 mg inserted nightly for 6 consecutive days.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard topical application.

max_recommended_dose: Topical and vaginal formulation; systemic absorption is clinically negligible (<0.5%).
side_effects: Local skin irritation, burning, erythema, mild stinging, peeling
precautions_contraindications: For topical/vaginal use only. Do not apply near eyes. Continue treatment for 1–2 weeks after symptoms resolve to prevent recurrence.
clinical_warning: If skin irritation or sensitization develops, discontinue use and consult a healthcare provider.

symptoms: Oral thrush with white removable plaques, vaginal itching with thick curdy discharge, fungal intertrigo in skin folds.
indication: Treatment of superficial candidiasis, mucosal candidal infections, and mixed dermatophyte skin infections.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.3 & Section 13.1
safety_note: Topical and oral gel preparations can potentiate anticoagulant effects of warfarin. Use appropriate formulation for the specific anatomical site (oral gel, vaginal cream, or topical cream).
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 11.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Cutaneous dermatophyte infections and superficial candidiasis
Oropharyngeal candidiasis (oral thrush)

dosage_by_age.children: Oral gel: small portion applied with clean finger to oral lesions 4 times daily after feeds in infants >4 months.
dosage_by_age.adults: Topical cream 2%: apply thinly to cleansed affected area twice daily for 2–4 weeks.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard topical application. Oral gel caution: potential drug interaction with oral anticoagulants.

max_recommended_dose: Topical application as directed.
side_effects: Local burning, contact dermatitis, itching
precautions_contraindications: Oral gel inhibits CYP2C9 and may severely augment warfarin anticoagulation. Topical forms should not contact eyes.
clinical_warning: Ensure complete course of therapy to prevent relapse.

symptoms: Honey-colored crusted erosions (impetigo), pustules, localized skin redness, infected minor cuts, folliculitis.
indication: Topical treatment of superficial primary bacterial skin infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 13.2 (Anti-infective medicines - Topical)
safety_note: Apply only to affected small surface areas as directed by a healthcare provider. Do not apply over extensive open burns or mucosal wounds. Avoid overuse to prevent bacterial resistance.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.5.6 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Impetigo and superficial bacterial skin infections caused by Staph and Strep
Eradication of nasal methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)

dosage_by_age.children: Apply small amount to affected area up to 3 times daily in infants >2 months.
dosage_by_age.adults: Apply small amount to affected area 2 to 3 times daily for up to 10 days. May cover with sterile dressing.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard application. Avoid large surface area application if renal impairment.

max_recommended_dose: Do not exceed 10 consecutive treatment days to minimize emergence of resistant strains.
side_effects: Local burning, stinging, itching, erythema at site of application
precautions_contraindications: Not for ophthalmic use. Contains polyethylene glycol; avoid on extensive open wounds in renal impairment.
clinical_warning: Limit treatment duration to 10 days to preserve antibacterial efficacy.

symptoms: Fever, painful swallowing, earache, tonsillar exudate, productive cough, or localized bacterial inflammatory signs.
indication: Treatment of susceptible bacterial infections of the upper respiratory tract, ear-nose-throat, and urinary tract.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.1 (Access Group Antibiotic)
safety_note: PRESCRIPTION REQUIRED. Strictly contraindicated in patients with known penicillin or beta-lactam hypersensitivity. Must complete the entire prescribed antibiotic course to prevent antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.2.1.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
strengths_available: Oral Liquid: 125 mg/5 mL (pediatric), 250 mg/5 mL (pediatric)
Powder for Injection: 250 mg, 500 mg, 1,000 mg
common_uses: Acute bacterial otitis media and streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis
Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia and lower respiratory infections
Acute bacterial sinusitis, dental infections, and uncomplicated cystitis

dosage_by_age.children: Oral suspension: 20–40 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours (or 40–90 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours for severe otitis/pneumonia) as prescribed by pediatrician.
dosage_by_age.adults: 250 mg to 500 mg orally every 8 hours, or 500 mg to 875 mg every 12 hours. Severe infections: up to 1,000 mg every 8 hours.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose; reduce dosing frequency in moderate-to-severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min).

max_recommended_dose: 3,000 mg (3 g) per day orally in adults; 90 mg/kg/day in children.
side_effects: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, erythematous skin rash
Antibiotic-associated colitis, oral and vaginal candidiasis
precautions_contraindications: STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in patients with verified penicillin or beta-lactam anaphylaxis history. High incidence of rash in infectious mononucleosis.
clinical_warning: Antibiotic prescription required. Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms resolve earlier to prevent bacterial resistance.

symptoms: Purulent sputum cough, fever, pleuritic chest tightness, tachypnea, crackles, acute bacterial sinusitis or otitis media.
indication: First-line empirical therapy for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, and otitis media.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.1
safety_note: Requires professional medical diagnosis (not indicated for common viral colds or flu). Watch for allergic reactions (skin rash, hives, wheezing, anaphylaxis). Complete the full prescribed course.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.2.1.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T

dosage_by_age.adults: 250 mg to 500 mg orally every 8 hours, or 500 mg to 875 mg every 12 hours. Severe infections: up to 1,000 mg every 8 hours.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose; reduce dosing frequency in moderate-to-severe renal impairment (GFR <30 mL/min).

max_recommended_dose: 3,000 mg (3 g) per day orally in adults; 90 mg/kg/day in children.
side_effects: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, erythematous skin rash
Antibiotic-associated colitis, oral and vaginal candidiasis

symptoms: Atypical pneumonia cough, bacterial pharyngitis in penicillin-allergic patients, chlamydial urethritis, skin soft-tissue infections.
indication: Treatment of atypical community-acquired pneumonia, sexually transmitted bacterial infections, and enteritis.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.1 (Watch Group Antibiotic)
safety_note: WHO Watch Group antibiotic — reserve for specific clinical indications under medical oversight to curb antibiotic resistance. Potential risk of QT cardiac interval prolongation and hepatic enzyme elevation.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.2.2.1, 6.7.6.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Community-acquired atypical pneumonia and acute bacterial bronchitis
Chlamydia trachomatis genital infections and enteric fever (typhoid)

dosage_by_age.children: Oral liquid: 10 mg/kg once daily on Day 1, followed by 5 mg/kg once daily on Days 2–5.
dosage_by_age.adults: Respiratory: 500 mg once daily on Day 1, then 250 mg once daily on Days 2–5 (or 500 mg daily for 3 days). STI (Chlamydia): 1,000 mg single dose.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose. Screen for baseline QT interval prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias.

max_recommended_dose: 500 mg/day for multi-day respiratory protocols; 1,000–2,000 mg single dose for specific STI regimens.
side_effects: Diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, QT prolongation
precautions_contraindications: Contraindicated in patients with cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction associated with prior macrolide use. Caution in arrhythmias and electrolyte imbalance.
clinical_warning: Prescription antibiotic. Take on an empty stomach or with light food if GI upset occurs.

symptoms: Tick bites with expanding rash (Lyme disease), rickettsial fever, severe inflammatory acne, atypical pelvic infections, malaria prophylaxis.
indication: Treatment of rickettsial diseases, chlamydia, mycoplasma pneumonia, severe acne vulgaris, and acute bacterial zoonoses.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.1 (Access Group Antibiotic)
safety_note: Contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 8 years due to permanent dental discoloration and bone growth effects. Take with a full glass of water sitting upright to prevent esophageal ulceration. Causes photosensitivity.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.2.2.7, 6.10.2.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Rickettsial diseases (scrub typhus, spotted fevers)
Atypical pneumonia, chlamydial urethritis, moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne
Malaria chemoprophylaxis for travelers

dosage_by_age.children: CONTRAINDICATED in children under 8 years due to permanent tooth staining and enamel hypoplasia (except in life-threatening rickettsial infections).
dosage_by_age.adults: 200 mg on day 1 (100 mg every 12 hours), followed by 100 mg once daily with meals and full glass of water.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dosage. Safe in renal impairment (eliminated via biliary route).

max_recommended_dose: 200 mg per 24 hours.
side_effects: Epigastric distress, esophageal ulceration (if taken recumbent), cutaneous photosensitivity
precautions_contraindications: Strictly contraindicated in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and children under 8 years. Take with large glass of water while upright and remain upright for 30 minutes.
clinical_warning: Avoid sun exposure due to photosensitivity risk. Ingest while standing with ample water.

symptoms: Dysuria (burning during urination), increased frequency, urinary urgency, suprapubic ache, cloudy or foul-smelling urine.
indication: First-line empirical treatment and prophylaxis of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections (acute cystitis).
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.1 (Access Group Antibacterial)
safety_note: Take with meals or milk to improve absorption and reduce nausea. Ineffective in systemic or upper tract infections (pyelonephritis). Contraindicated in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) and late-stage pregnancy.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.2.2.10 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Treatment of uncomplicated acute lower urinary tract infections (cystitis)
Long-term prophylaxis of recurrent urinary tract infections

dosage_by_age.children: Infants >3 months: 3–5 mg/kg/day divided in 4 doses with food. Contraindicated in infants <1 month.
dosage_by_age.adults: Macrobid formulation: 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days with food. Monohydrate: 50–100 mg 4 times daily for 7 days.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Contraindicated if eGFR <45 mL/min due to poor urinary concentration and high risk of neuro/pulmonary toxicity.

max_recommended_dose: 400 mg per 24 hours.
side_effects: Dark yellow/brown urine discoloration (benign), nausea, headache, peripheral neuropathy
precautions_contraindications: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment (eGFR <45 mL/min), G6PD deficiency, and term pregnancy (weeks 38–42).
clinical_warning: Not indicated for upper tract kidney infections (pyelonephritis). Take with meals.

symptoms: Foul-smelling dental abscesses, intra-abdominal infections, bacterial vaginosis (fishy discharge), amoebic dysentery, giardiasis.
indication: Eradication of anaerobic bacterial infections, surgical prophylaxis, amoebiasis, giardiasis, and trichomoniasis.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.1 (Access Group)
safety_note: STRICTLY AVOID ALL ALCOHOL during therapy and for 48 hours afterwards due to severe disulfiram-like reactions (vomiting, flushing, tachycardia). Metallic taste is common. Medical prescription mandatory.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.2.2.9, 6.9.1.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Intestinal and hepatic amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica)
Giardiasis, trichomoniasis, and bacterial vaginosis
Anaerobic bacterial intra-abdominal, pelvic, and dental infections

dosage_by_age.children: Amoebiasis: 35–50 mg/kg/day divided in 3 doses for 7–10 days. Giardiasis: 15 mg/kg/day for 5 days.
dosage_by_age.adults: Amoebic dysentery: 400–800 mg 3 times daily for 7–10 days. Trichomoniasis: 2 g single dose or 400 mg twice daily for 7 days.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose; reduce dose by 50% in severe hepatic failure.

max_recommended_dose: 2,400 mg/24h for oral therapy.
side_effects: Unpleasant metallic taste, dark reddish-brown urine, nausea, anorexia, peripheral neuropathy with prolonged therapy
precautions_contraindications: ABSOLUTELY AVOID ALCOHOL during therapy and for 48 hours after (disulfiram-like severe reaction). History of active neurological disorders.
clinical_warning: Strict abstinence from alcohol required during treatment to prevent severe nausea, flushing, and tachycardia.

symptoms: Cellulitis, red swollen skin lesions, folliculitis, uncomplicated urinary tract symptoms, streptococcal throat infections.
indication: Treatment of susceptible gram-positive skin and soft-tissue infections, bone infections, and uncomplicated cystitis.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.1 (Access Group)
safety_note: Caution in patients with mild penicillin allergies (cross-reactivity risk ~1-3%). Strictly avoid if history of severe immediate penicillin anaphylaxis. Must complete full duration of prescription.
nlem_reference: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) Section 6.2.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
strengths_available: Oral Liquid: 125 mg/5 mL (pediatric), 250 mg/5 mL (pediatric)
common_uses: Bacterial skin and soft tissue infections (cellulitis, folliculitis)
Streptococcal pharyngitis, mild otitis media, uncomplicated urinary infections

dosage_by_age.children: 25–50 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 12 hours (up to 100 mg/kg/day in severe skin infections).
dosage_by_age.adults: 250 mg to 500 mg orally every 6 hours, or 500 mg every 12 hours for 7–14 days.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose; adjust interval in severe renal failure.

max_recommended_dose: 4,000 mg (4 g) per 24 hours.
side_effects: Diarrhea, nausea, dyspepsia, mild allergic rash
precautions_contraindications: Cephalosporin allergy or severe immediate penicillin anaphylaxis history. Complete the prescribed course.
clinical_warning: Antibiotic requiring verified medical diagnosis.

symptoms: Chronic persistent cough (>2-3 weeks), haemoptysis (coughing blood), night sweats, weight loss, low-grade evening fever.
indication: Core component of multi-drug regimens for active pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis; also used for latent TB preventive therapy.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.4 (Antituberculosis medicines)
safety_note: Strictly administered under national TB guidelines or Directly Observed Therapy (DOTS). Co-administer Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) to prevent peripheral neuropathy. Monitor liver function tests (risk of drug-induced hepatitis).
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.4.9 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Active tuberculosis treatment (in combination with Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol)
Latent tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT)

dosage_by_age.children: 10–15 mg/kg once daily (max 300 mg/day) as part of national pediatric TB regimen.
dosage_by_age.adults: 300 mg once daily (or 5 mg/kg/day) taken on an empty stomach.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard weight-based dose; mandatory co-administration of Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) to prevent neurotoxicity.

max_recommended_dose: 300 mg/day in daily therapy.
side_effects: Peripheral neuropathy (numbness/tingling), elevated liver enzymes, drug-induced hepatitis
precautions_contraindications: Acute liver disease, chronic alcohol abuse. Co-prescribe Pyridoxine (10–25 mg/day) routinely.
clinical_warning: Prescription anti-tubercular medication under National TB Elimination Program guidelines.

symptoms: Productive cough with sputum/blood, chest pains, systemic fatigue, cachexia, chronic fever in confirmed TB infection.
indication: Essential first-line bactericidal component in multi-drug treatment regimens for active tuberculosis and leprosy.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 6.2.4
safety_note: Must never be used as monotherapy for active TB to avoid rapid drug resistance. Harmlessly turns urine, tears, sweat, and saliva orange-red. Strong inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (major drug interactions with oral contraceptives, antiretrovirals, warfarin).
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 6.3.3, 6.4.15 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: First-line multidrug treatment of tuberculosis and leprosy
Meningococcal meningitis contact prophylaxis

dosage_by_age.children: 10–20 mg/kg once daily (max 600 mg/day) on an empty stomach.
dosage_by_age.adults: 450 mg (<50 kg) or 600 mg (≥50 kg) once daily on an empty stomach.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard weight-based dose; extensive monitoring for hepatic enzymes and drug interactions.

max_recommended_dose: 600 mg/day.
side_effects: Reddish-orange discoloration of urine, sweat, tears, and saliva (harmless)
Hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal intolerance, thrombocytopenia
precautions_contraindications: Potent hepatic CYP3A4 enzyme inducer (drastically reduces levels of oral contraceptives, warfarin, antiretrovirals, diabetes oral agents).
clinical_warning: Urine and tears will turn orange-red. Use alternative non-hormonal contraception.

symptoms: Acute shortness of breath, audible expiratory wheezing, chest tightness, coughing spasms triggered by exercise or allergens.
indication: Rapid relief of acute bronchospasm, asthma attacks, and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 25.1 (Medicines for asthma and COPD)
safety_note: Quick-relief inhaler for acute symptoms, not an anti-inflammatory controller. Over-reliance (>2-3 times/week) signals poorly controlled asthma needing inhaled corticosteroid adjustment. Transient tremor or mild tachycardia may occur.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 24.1.6 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Quick-relief bronchodilator for acute asthma bronchospasm
Reversible airway obstruction in COPD and acute wheezing
Prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm

dosage_by_age.children: Inhaler: 1–2 puffs (100–200 mcg) via spacer as needed for acute wheeze. Nebulizer: 2.5 mg under hospital emergency monitoring.
dosage_by_age.adults: Inhaler: 1–2 puffs (100–200 mcg) as needed for acute breathlessness; max 4 times daily (8 puffs/day). Nebulizer: 2.5–5 mg for acute exacerbations.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Inhalation route strictly preferred over oral tablets to minimize tachycardia and cardiac arrhythmia risk.

max_recommended_dose: Inhaler: 800 mcg (8 puffs) in 24 hours under outpatient conditions.
side_effects: Fine skeletal muscle tremor (especially hands), tachycardia, palpitations, headache, hypokalemia
precautions_contraindications: Cardiac arrhythmias, hypertension, hyperthyroidism. Frequent need (>3 times/week) indicates uncontrolled asthma requiring inhaled corticosteroid controller therapy.
clinical_warning: Rescue inhaler only; does not treat underlying airway inflammation. Seek emergency care if symptoms do not improve after 4 puffs.

symptoms: Frequent nocturnal awakening with cough, chronic daily wheeze, variable airway hyperresponsiveness, exercise limitation.
indication: Daily maintenance controller therapy for persistent chronic asthma to reduce airway inflammation and prevent exacerbations.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 25.1
safety_note: Must be used regularly every day as prescribed; not intended for immediate relief during an acute attack. Rinse mouth with water and spit out after inhalation to prevent oral candidiasis (thrush) and hoarseness.
nlem_reference: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) Section 25.1 / Budesonide NLEM Section 16.1, 24.1.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Daily maintenance and controller therapy for persistent asthma
Allergic rhinitis prophylaxis (nasal formulation)

dosage_by_age.children: Inhalation: 50–100 mcg twice daily with metered-dose inhaler and spacer.
dosage_by_age.adults: Inhalation: 100–400 mcg twice daily based on severity of asthma.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard dosage with spacer device.

max_recommended_dose: Up to 1,000–2,000 mcg/day in severe persistent asthma under pulmonologist care.
side_effects: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (oral thrush), hoarseness (dysphonia), throat irritation
precautions_contraindications: Not a rescue inhaler (slow onset). Rinse mouth with water and spit out after each use to prevent fungal oral thrush.
clinical_warning: Must be taken consistently every day, even when feeling well, to prevent asthma exacerbations.

symptoms: Chronic progressive breathlessness, productive morning cough, chronic wheezing, reduced exercise capacity in smokers/exposed individuals.
indication: Symptomatic relief of reversible airway obstruction and acute exacerbations in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 25.1
safety_note: Use with spacer device for improved lung deposition. Frequent acute exacerbations in COPD require physician evaluation for long-acting bronchodilators, pulmonary rehab, and smoking cessation.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 24.1.6 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T

Reversible airway obstruction in COPD and acute wheezing
Prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm

clinical_warning: Rescue inhaler only; does not treat underlying airway inflammation. Seek emergency care if symptoms do not improve after 4 puffs.

symptoms: Bouts of sneezing, clear runny rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, itchy palate, red watery itchy eyes.
indication: Symptomatic relief of seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever), perennial allergic rhinitis, and chronic urticaria.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 3.1 (Antiallergics and anaphylaxis medicines)
safety_note: Less sedating than first-generation antihistamines, but mild drowsiness may still occur in some individuals. Avoid alcohol and exercise caution when driving. Dose adjustment needed in moderate-to-severe renal failure.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 3.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Allergic rhinitis (sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal itching)
Chronic idiopathic urticaria (hives, skin welts)
Allergic conjunctivitis and pruritus

dosage_by_age.children: Children 2–6 years: 2.5 mg twice daily (or 5 mg once daily); 6–12 years: 5 mg twice daily (or 10 mg once daily).
dosage_by_age.adults: 10 mg once daily orally (or 5 mg twice daily) with water.
dosage_by_age.elderly: 5 mg once daily starting dose; adjust according to renal clearance.

max_recommended_dose: 10 mg per 24 hours.
side_effects: Mild drowsiness, dry mouth, headache, fatigue, dizziness
precautions_contraindications: End-stage renal disease (GFR <10 mL/min). Avoid alcohol and central sedatives. Caution when driving or operating machinery.
clinical_warning: Second-generation antihistamine with low sedation, but individual sensitivity varies. Take at bedtime if drowsiness occurs.

symptoms: Itchy wheals/hives on skin (urticaria), facial redness, itchy watery eyes, allergic pruritus.
indication: Relief of symptoms associated with allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, and chronic idiopathic urticaria.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 3.1
safety_note: Non-sedating at standard recommended doses. If severe swelling of the lips, tongue, throat or breathing difficulty occurs (anaphylaxis), call emergency services (108/112) immediately — antihistamines alone are insufficient.
nlem_reference: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) Section 3.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Seasonal allergic rhinitis and perennial allergic rhinitis
Chronic idiopathic urticaria and allergic skin reactions

dosage_by_age.children: Children 2–12 years: 5 mg once daily (<30 kg) or 10 mg once daily (>30 kg).
dosage_by_age.adults: 10 mg once daily.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard adult dose of 10 mg once daily (non-sedating profile).

max_recommended_dose: 10 mg per 24 hours.
side_effects: Headache, dry mouth, fatigue, rare GI discomfort
precautions_contraindications: Severe hepatic impairment (start at 10 mg every other day). Non-sedating antihistamine.
clinical_warning: Non-drowsy allergy relief. Consult a doctor if hives persist beyond 6 weeks.

symptoms: Often asymptomatic ('silent killer'); may present with occipital morning headache, dizziness, fatigue, or elevated sphygmomanometer readings.
indication: First-line pharmacotherapy for essential hypertension and chronic stable coronary angina pectoris.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 12.3 (Antihypertensive medicines)
safety_note: PRESCRIPTION ONLY. Do not stop abruptly. Peripheral bilateral ankle swelling (edema), flushing, and dizziness may occur. Regular blood pressure monitoring and physician follow-up required.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 10.3.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Essential systemic hypertension
Chronic stable angina pectoris and vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina

dosage_by_age.children: 2.5 mg once daily, titrated to max 5 mg daily in children 6–17 years under pediatric cardiologist supervision.
dosage_by_age.adults: Initial: 5 mg once daily; may be titrated after 1–2 weeks to maximum 10 mg once daily.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Initial: 2.5 mg once daily recommended due to reduced hepatic clearance and peripheral edema risk.

max_recommended_dose: 10 mg per 24 hours.
side_effects: Peripheral edema (bilateral ankle swelling), flushing, dizziness, headache, palpitations
precautions_contraindications: Severe aortic stenosis, severe hypotension, unstable heart failure after MI. Do not discontinue abruptly.
clinical_warning: Long-acting calcium channel blocker. Blood pressure monitoring is mandatory.

symptoms: Persistently elevated blood pressure (>140/90 mmHg), hypertensive target organ risk, microalbuminuria in diabetes.
indication: Management of essential hypertension, congestive heart failure, and prevention of renal disease in diabetic patients.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 12.3
safety_note: STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (teratogenic / fetal toxicity). A persistent dry tickly cough occurs in ~10-15% of patients. Monitor baseline serum potassium and renal function (creatinine/eGFR).
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 10.3.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T

Diabetic nephropathy in type 1 and type 2 diabetes

dosage_by_age.adults: Initial: 5 mg once daily (2.5 mg if on diuretic). Maintenance: 10–20 mg once daily or divided.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Initial: 2.5 mg once daily; monitor renal function and serum potassium.

max_recommended_dose: 40 mg per 24 hours.
side_effects: Persistent dry non-productive cough, dizziness, hypotension, hyperkalemia, angioedema
precautions_contraindications: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY (fetotoxic: renal dysgenesis, skull hypoplasia). Bilateral renal artery stenosis. History of ACE inhibitor angioedema.
clinical_warning: ACE inhibitor requiring baseline creatinine and potassium checks. Discontinue immediately if pregnancy occurs.

symptoms: High blood pressure readings, mild fluid retention, requiring combination antihypertensive therapy.
indication: Treatment of arterial hypertension and mild fluid retention (edema) due to heart failure or renal disorders.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 12.3
safety_note: Take in the morning to prevent nocturnal urination. Periodic laboratory monitoring of electrolytes (risk of hypokalemia, hyponatremia) and blood glucose/uric acid levels is recommended.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 10.3.3, 15.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Essential hypertension (monotherapy or combined with ACEI/ARB/CCB)
Edema associated with congestive heart failure and hepatic cirrhosis

dosage_by_age.children: 1–2 mg/kg/day in 1 or 2 divided doses.
dosage_by_age.adults: Hypertension: 12.5 mg to 25 mg once daily in the morning. Edema: 25–50 mg daily.
dosage_by_age.elderly: 12.5 mg once daily; heightened susceptibility to hyponatremia and hypokalemia.

max_recommended_dose: 50 mg per 24 hours.
side_effects: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia (gout flare), hyperglycemia, photosensitivity
precautions_contraindications: Anuria, severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min), refractory hypokalemia/hyponatremia, active gout. Take in morning to prevent nighttime urination.
clinical_warning: Thiazide diuretic. Periodic electrolyte monitoring is required.

symptoms: Bilateral pedal pitting edema, shortness of breath when lying flat (orthopnea), acute nocturnal dyspnea, fluid overload.
indication: Rapid diuresis and relief of fluid overload in acute and chronic heart failure, pulmonary edema, nephrotic syndrome, and hepatic cirrhosis.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 16.1 (Diuretics)
safety_note: POTENT DIURETIC. Strict medical dosing required. Can cause profound electrolyte loss (potassium, sodium, magnesium), hypotension, and dehydration. Monitor daily weights and serum biochemistry.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 15.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Acute pulmonary edema and fluid retention in congestive heart failure
Chronic renal failure edema and nephrotic syndrome
Cirrhotic ascites (combined with spironolactone)

dosage_by_age.children: 1–2 mg/kg per dose orally or IV; maximum 6 mg/kg/day.
dosage_by_age.adults: 20 mg to 40 mg once daily in the morning; dose titrated upward in resistant edema under medical monitoring.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Initial 20 mg daily; monitor for orthostatic hypotension, dehydration, and electrolyte depletion.

max_recommended_dose: Up to 600 mg/day in severe oliguric renal failure under hospital monitoring.
side_effects: Profound diuresis, dehydration, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypotension, ototoxicity at high IV doses
precautions_contraindications: Anuria, severe hypokalemia, hepatic coma, sulfonamide allergy. Potassium supplementation or monitoring usually required.
clinical_warning: Potent loop diuretic. Requires close clinical and laboratory monitoring.

symptoms: Elevated fasting blood sugar, polyuria (frequent urination), polydipsia (excessive thirst), weight loss, chronic fatigue.
indication: First-line oral pharmacotherapy for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus in conjunction with diet and physical activity.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 18.5 (Medicines for diabetes)
safety_note: Take with or after meals to decrease gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, diarrhea). Contraindicated in severe renal failure (eGFR <30 mL/min) or severe hypoxic states due to risk of lactic acidosis.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 18.3.1.6 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: First-line oral pharmacotherapy for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) insulin resistance management

dosage_by_age.children: Children ≥10 years: 500 mg once or twice daily with meals (max 2,000 mg/day).
dosage_by_age.adults: Initial: 500 mg once or twice daily with meals. Titrated weekly by 500 mg to 1,000 mg twice daily.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Assess eGFR prior to initiation. Contraindicated if eGFR <30 mL/min; max 1,000 mg/day if eGFR 30–44 mL/min.

max_recommended_dose: 2,550 mg/day (immediate release) or 2,000 mg/day (extended release).
side_effects: Gastrointestinal disturbance (diarrhea, nausea, abdominal cramping, metallic taste)
Long-term: Vitamin B12 malabsorption. Rare: lactic acidosis.
precautions_contraindications: Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min), acute metabolic acidosis, severe hypoxemia, acute heart failure. Withhold 48h before IV iodinated contrast.
clinical_warning: Take with or immediately after meals to reduce stomach upset. Never take if severely dehydrated or acutely ill.

symptoms: Marked hyperglycemia, ketonuria, rapid weight loss, polyphagia, diabetic ketoacidosis, or failure of oral agents.
indication: Essential glycemic management in Type 1 diabetes, gestational diabetes, and uncontrolled or advanced Type 2 diabetes.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 18.5
safety_note: CRITICAL: Patient education on blood glucose monitoring and injection technique is mandatory. High risk of hypoglycemia (shakiness, sweating, confusion, coma) if missed meals or overdosed. Store in refrigerator (2-8°C).
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 18.3.1.2, 18.3.1.3, 18.3.1.4, 18.3.1.5 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
strengths_available: Injection 40 IU/mL: Soluble (Regular), Intermediate Acting (NPH), Premix 30:70
common_uses: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (absolute insulin deficiency)
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus inadequately controlled on oral agents
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Gestational diabetes

dosage_by_age.children: Strictly individualized regimen (typically 0.5–1.0 IU/kg/day) based on frequent self-monitoring of blood glucose under pediatric endocrinologist direction.
dosage_by_age.adults: Individualized regimen: basal insulin once daily plus prandial regular insulin before meals, adjusted by blood glucose targets.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Relaxed glycemic targets (HbA1c 7.5–8.0%) to prevent fatal hypoglycemia.

max_recommended_dose: Individualized to achieve target blood glucose without causing hypoglycemia.
side_effects: Hypoglycemia (sweating, palpitations, confusion, coma), lipodystrophy at injection sites, weight gain
precautions_contraindications: Hypoglycemia episodes. Always carry fast-acting carbohydrates. Rotate injection sites. Store unopened vials at 2–8°C; in-use vial at room temperature <30°C for up to 28 days.
clinical_warning: CRITICAL: Never adjust insulin doses without doctor guidance. Skipping meals after injection causes dangerous hypoglycemia.

symptoms: Chronic fatigue, unexplainable weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, bradycardia, puffy face, hair loss.
indication: Replacement or supplemental therapy in congenital or acquired primary and secondary hypothyroidism.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 18.8 (Thyroid hormones and antithyroid medicines)
safety_note: Take on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, ideally 30-60 minutes before breakfast. Avoid taking with calcium, iron, or antacids within 4 hours. Regular serum TSH testing is needed to titrate dosage.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 18.6.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
strengths_available: Tablet: 12.5 mcg, 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 62.5 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 150 mcg
common_uses: Primary, secondary, and tertiary hypothyroidism
Congenital hypothyroidism in neonates and infants
TSH suppression in differentiated thyroid cancer

dosage_by_age.children: Congenital hypothyroidism: 10–15 mcg/kg/day immediately upon birth under pediatric endocrinologist guidance.
dosage_by_age.adults: 1.6 mcg/kg/day (typically 50–100 mcg once daily), taken on an empty stomach with plain water 30–60 minutes before breakfast.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Start low (12.5–25 mcg/day) and titrate slowly by 12.5–25 mcg increments every 6–8 weeks to avoid precipitating myocardial ischemia.

max_recommended_dose: Individualized based on serum TSH normalization (typically 200–300 mcg/day max).
side_effects: Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis from overtreatment: palpitations, tachycardia, insomnia, tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance
precautions_contraindications: Untreated subclinical thyrotoxicosis, acute myocardial infarction, uncorrected adrenal insufficiency. Separate by 4 hours from calcium and iron supplements.
clinical_warning: Take once daily in the morning on an empty stomach with plain water. Routine TSH monitoring required.

symptoms: Focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic convulsions with loss of consciousness, involuntary limb jerking, post-ictal confusion.
indication: Control of focal (partial) and generalized tonic-clonic epileptic seizures; also first-line for trigeminal neuralgia.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 5.1 (Anticonvulsants / Antiepileptics)
safety_note: SPECIALIST GUIDANCE REQUIRED. Never discontinue abruptly (may precipitate status epilepticus). Monitor blood counts and liver enzymes. Watch for severe dermatological reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), especially in genetically predisposed populations.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 5.1.1, 23.2.2.3 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures in epilepsy
Trigeminal neuralgia pain paroxysms
Bipolar disorder acute mania and mood stabilization

dosage_by_age.children: 10–20 mg/kg/day divided in 2–3 doses, titrated upward gradually under neurologist supervision.
dosage_by_age.adults: Epilepsy: initial 100–200 mg 1–2 times daily, titrated to 800–1,200 mg/day in divided doses. Trigeminal neuralgia: 100 mg twice daily titrated to relief.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Start at 100 mg daily; high vulnerability to hyponatremia and drug-drug interactions.

max_recommended_dose: 1,600 mg/day for epilepsy; 1,200 mg/day for trigeminal neuralgia.
side_effects: Dizziness, ataxia, drowsiness, diplopia, hyponatremia (SIADH), leukopenia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)
precautions_contraindications: Atrioventricular conduction block, history of bone marrow depression. Genetic screening for HLA-B*1502 in Asian patients strongly recommended before initiation.
clinical_warning: Narrow therapeutic index antiepileptic. Do not stop taking abruptly as this can trigger status epilepticus.

symptoms: Absence seizures (blank staring spells), myoclonic jerks, generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
indication: Treatment of generalized, focal, and mixed epileptic seizures; also used in acute manic episodes of bipolar disorder.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 5.1
safety_note: HIGH TERATOGENIC RISK: Strictly contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless strict pregnancy prevention program conditions are met (causes neural tube defects and developmental disorders). Monitor liver function.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 5.1.10, 23.2.2.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Broad-spectrum antiepileptic (absence, myoclonic, tonic-clonic, focal seizures)
Bipolar disorder acute manic episodes
Migraine headache prophylaxis

dosage_by_age.children: Initial: 10–15 mg/kg/day divided in 2 doses; maintenance 20–30 mg/kg/day under pediatric neurologist guidance.
dosage_by_age.adults: Initial: 600 mg daily divided in 2 doses; maintenance 1,000–2,000 mg daily.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Start at 250–500 mg daily; monitor free valproate levels due to decreased plasma protein binding.

max_recommended_dose: 2,500 mg/day (or 60 mg/kg/day under therapeutic drug monitoring).
side_effects: Weight gain, fine postural tremor, transient hair loss, nausea, thrombocytopenia, fatal pancreatitis / hepatotoxicity
precautions_contraindications: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY (high risk of congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental delays). Active liver disease. Mitochondrial disorders.
clinical_warning: Pregnancy prevention program mandatory for female patients. Baseline liver function tests required.

symptoms: Low mood, persistent insomnia, chronic neuropathic burning pain, somatic anxiety symptoms, loss of interest.
indication: Treatment of major depressive episodes, neuropathic pain, and tension headache/migraine prophylaxis.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 24.2.1 (Medicines for depressive disorders)
safety_note: Sedating — take at bedtime. Causes anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention). Cardiotoxic in overdose (QT prolongation, arrhythmias). Close clinical monitoring required.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 5.2.1.1, 7.4.2, 23.2.1.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Major depressive disorder
Chronic neuropathic pain (diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia)
Migraine headache prophylaxis and tension headache prevention
Fibromyalgia and chronic musculoskeletal pain syndromes

dosage_by_age.children: Not recommended for depression under 18 years. Migraine prophylaxis in adolescents only under child neurologist guidance.
dosage_by_age.adults: Neuropathic pain/Migraine: 10–25 mg at bedtime, titrated by 10–25 mg every 1–2 weeks to 25–75 mg at bedtime. Depression: 50–150 mg at bedtime.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Initial 10 mg at bedtime; high risk of anticholinergic side effects (confusion, urinary retention, orthostatic hypotension, falls).

max_recommended_dose: 150 mg/day (inpatient psychiatric: up to 200 mg/day).
side_effects: Dry mouth, marked sedation, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias
precautions_contraindications: Recent myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, heart block, narrow-angle glaucoma, severe liver disease. Never combine with MAO inhibitors.
clinical_warning: Causes significant nighttime sedation. Take 1–2 hours before bedtime. Do not drive if drowsy.

symptoms: Pervasive sadness, anhedonia (inability to feel pleasure), feelings of worthlessness, fatigue, changes in sleep and appetite.
indication: Treatment of major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and panic disorder.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 24.2.1
safety_note: Therapeutic response typically requires 2 to 4 weeks of consistent administration. Monitor closely for paradoxical behavioral changes or increased agitation in early weeks. Do not combine with MAO inhibitors or other serotonergic agents (serotonin syndrome risk).
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 7.4.6, 23.2.1.3, 23.4.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Major depressive disorder
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
Bulimia nervosa and panic disorder

dosage_by_age.children: Children ≥8 years with moderate-to-severe depression: 10–20 mg once daily under child psychiatrist monitoring.
dosage_by_age.adults: 20 mg once daily in the morning; may be titrated after several weeks up to 40–60 mg daily for OCD or refractory depression.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Initial 10 mg once daily; max recommended 40 mg daily.

max_recommended_dose: 80 mg per 24 hours.
side_effects: Nausea, insomnia, anxiety, headache, anorexia, sexual dysfunction, hyponatremia
precautions_contraindications: Concurrent use with MAOIs (contraindicated, risk of fatal Serotonin Syndrome). Monitor young patients closely for emergent suicidal ideation during early treatment.
clinical_warning: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). Requires 2–4 weeks to achieve therapeutic antidepressant effect.

symptoms: Frequent, recurrent, debilitating migraine attacks (>3-4 disabling attacks per month), visual disturbance, pulsating head pain.
indication: Long-term prophylaxis of recurrent migraine headaches; also used in essential tremor and situational somatic anxiety.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 7.2 (Medicines for migraine prophylaxis)
safety_note: CONTRAINDICATED in bronchial asthma, severe COPD, bradycardia, and high-degree heart block due to bronchospasm and conduction slowing risks. Do not stop abruptly; requires gradual tapering.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 5.2.1.3 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Migraine headache prophylaxis
Essential tremor and somatic symptoms of performance anxiety
Hypertension, angina pectoris, supraventricular arrhythmias, thyrotoxicosis

dosage_by_age.children: Infantile hemangioma / pediatric arrhythmias: under specialist pediatric cardiology protocol only.
dosage_by_age.adults: Migraine prevention: 40 mg 2–3 times daily (titrated to 80–160 mg daily). Performance anxiety: 10–40 mg 1 hour before event.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Start at 10–20 mg daily; high susceptibility to bradycardia, fatigue, and hypotension.

max_recommended_dose: 240 mg/day for migraine prophylaxis; 320 mg/day for cardiovascular indications.
side_effects: Bradycardia, cold extremities, fatigue, sleep disturbances, bronchospasm in susceptible individuals
precautions_contraindications: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED IN BRONCHIAL ASTHMA and severe COPD (can trigger fatal bronchospasm). Sinus bradycardia, cardiogenic shock. Do not stop abruptly.
clinical_warning: Non-selective beta-blocker. Strictly contraindicated in asthmatic patients.

symptoms: Recurrent attacks of excruciating monoarticular joint pain, hyperuricemia, tophi deposits, history of gouty arthritis.
indication: Long-term reduction of serum and urinary uric acid levels for prevention of gout flare-ups and renal uric acid stones.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 2.3 (Medicines for gout)
safety_note: DO NOT initiate during an acute gout flare (may paradoxically prolong the acute attack). Ensure adequate hydration (2-3 L/day). Discontinue immediately and seek emergency care if an unexplained skin rash or allergic sign develops.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 2.3.1, 7.4.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Chronic management of primary and secondary hyperuricemia in gout
Prevention of recurrent uric acid kidney stones
Prophylaxis of tumor lysis syndrome in chemotherapy

dosage_by_age.children: Secondary hyperuricemia in pediatric malignancies: 10–20 mg/kg/day under pediatric oncology care.
dosage_by_age.adults: Initial: 100 mg once daily after food; titrate weekly by 100 mg to achieve serum urate <6 mg/dL (maintenance 200–300 mg daily).
dosage_by_age.elderly: Initial: 50–100 mg daily; adjust strictly according to creatinine clearance.

max_recommended_dose: 800 mg/day (or 300 mg/day in moderate renal impairment).
side_effects: Maculopapular rash, gastrointestinal distress, acute gout flare precipitation (co-prescribe colchicine), severe hypersensitivity syndrome
precautions_contraindications: DO NOT INITIATE DURING AN ACUTE GOUT FLARE (wait until acute inflammation subsides). Discontinue immediately at first sign of skin rash.
clinical_warning: Urate-lowering therapy must not be started during an acute painful gout attack. Drink plenty of water.

symptoms: Sudden onset of severe, excruciating pain, redness, hot swelling in the first metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe) or ankle.
indication: Treatment of acute gouty arthritis flares and prophylaxis of recurrent gout flares during initiation of urate-lowering therapy.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 2.3
safety_note: Narrow therapeutic index: avoid excessive dosing. Gastrointestinal toxicity (diarrhea, abdominal cramps, vomiting) is the early sign of toxicity. Dose reduction required in renal or hepatic impairment.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 2.3.2 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Acute relief of painful gout flares
Prophylaxis of acute gout flares during initiation of allopurinol
Familial Mediterranean fever

dosage_by_age.children: Familial Mediterranean fever: under pediatric specialist care only.
dosage_by_age.adults: Acute gout: 1 mg (two 0.5 mg tablets) immediately at symptom onset, followed by 0.5 mg one hour later. No further doses for 12 hours. Prophylaxis: 0.5 mg 1–2 times daily.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Dose reduction mandatory (0.5 mg max initial); high risk of cumulative neuromuscular toxicity and drug interactions.

max_recommended_dose: 1.5 mg total per acute attack course; must not repeat course within 3 days.
side_effects: Diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting (toxicity indicators), neuromuscular weakness
precautions_contraindications: Narrow therapeutic window. Severe renal or hepatic impairment (contraindicated with macrolides like clarithromycin). Stop immediately if diarrhea occurs.
clinical_warning: Toxic in overdose. Stop taking immediately and call a doctor if diarrhea, nausea, or abdominal pain occurs.

symptoms: Pallor (pale skin/conjunctiva), severe fatigue, exertional dyspnea, dizziness, brittle nails, restless legs, low haemoglobin/ferritin.
indication: Prevention and treatment of microcytic iron deficiency anaemia in adults, pregnant women, and pediatric patients.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 10.1 (Antianaemia medicines)
safety_note: May cause harmless black-colored stools, constipation, or mild gastric irritation. Vitamin C enhances absorption; avoid taking simultaneously with tea, coffee, milk, or antacids. Keep strictly out of reach of children (pediatric iron toxicity is dangerous).
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 8.1.2, 8.1.3 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
strengths_available: Tablet: Equivalent to 60 mg elemental iron
common_uses: Treatment and prevention of iron-deficiency anemia
Maternal nutritional supplementation during pregnancy and lactation

dosage_by_age.children: Treatment of iron deficiency: 3–6 mg elemental iron/kg/day divided in 2–3 doses between meals.
dosage_by_age.adults: Therapeutic: 100–200 mg elemental iron daily in divided doses. Prophylactic: 60 mg elemental iron daily.
dosage_by_age.elderly: 60–100 mg elemental iron daily; high rate of constipation and gastrointestinal intolerance.

max_recommended_dose: 200 mg elemental iron daily for treatment.
side_effects: Dark green or black stools (harmless), constipation, nausea, abdominal discomfort, heartburn
precautions_contraindications: Hemochromatosis, chronic hemolytic anemia. KEEP OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN (accidental iron ingestion in young children is a fatal emergency). Take with Vitamin C for absorption.
clinical_warning: Stools will turn harmlessly black. Accidental overdose in toddlers is life-threatening.

symptoms: Macrocytic anaemia, glossitis (smooth red sore tongue), mouth ulcers, maternal preconception neural tube defect prevention.
indication: Treatment of folate deficiency megaloblastic anaemia; essential periconceptional supplementation to prevent fetal neural tube defects.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 10.1
safety_note: Well tolerated. When treating megaloblastic anaemia, ensure Vitamin B12 deficiency is ruled out first, as folic acid alone can correct haematological parameters while allowing irreversible neurological damage of B12 deficiency to progress.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 8.1.3, 8.1.4 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency
Prevention of neural tube defects (NTDs) in women planning pregnancy
Toxicity prophylaxis in patients on methotrexate

dosage_by_age.children: 1–5 mg once daily for folate deficiency until full hematological recovery.
dosage_by_age.adults: Treatment: 5 mg daily for 4 months. Pregnancy prophylaxis: 0.4–1 mg daily (5 mg daily in high-risk women with prior NTD).
dosage_by_age.elderly: 1–5 mg daily; always verify Vitamin B12 status before high-dose folate to prevent irreversible neurological damage.

max_recommended_dose: 5 mg/day (15 mg/day in severe malabsorption).
side_effects: Extremely well tolerated. Very rare mild gastrointestinal symptoms, hypersensitivity
precautions_contraindications: Never administer folic acid alone in undiagnosed megaloblastic anemia without ruling out Vitamin B12 deficiency (can mask B12-induced subacute combined cord degeneration).
clinical_warning: Vitamin B12 deficiency must be ruled out before initiating high-dose folic acid.

symptoms: Pruritic erythematous skin patches, atopic eczema, contact dermatitis, insect bite reactions, mild allergic rash.
indication: Symptomatic short-term relief of mild-to-moderate inflammatory, allergic, and pruritic non-infected dermatoses.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 13.3 (Anti-inflammatory and antipruritic medicines)
safety_note: Do not use on infected skin (fungal, viral, or untreated bacterial infections). Avoid prolonged continuous application (>1-2 weeks) on thin facial skin or under occlusive dressings to prevent skin thinning (atrophy) or striae.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 3.4, 18.1.3, 24.1.3 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Topical: mild eczema, contact dermatitis, insect bites, and inflammatory rashes
Systemic: acute adrenal insufficiency, severe anaphylaxis, septic shock, status asthmaticus

dosage_by_age.children: Topical 1%: apply thinly once or twice daily for up to 7 days. Avoid prolonged use on diaper area.
dosage_by_age.adults: Topical: apply sparingly 1–2 times daily for 1–2 weeks. Systemic IV: 100–200 mg every 6 hours in acute crisis under hospital supervision.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Topical: use lowest potency and shortest duration to prevent skin thinning and purpura.

max_recommended_dose: Topical: limited area. Systemic: determined by clinical crisis severity.
side_effects: Topical: local skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, secondary skin infection. Systemic: hypertension, hyperglycemia.
precautions_contraindications: Do not apply to infected skin (viral, bacterial, fungal) without antimicrobial coverage. Avoid face and eyes.
clinical_warning: Mild topical steroid. Do not use on infected or ulcerated skin.

symptoms: Intense nocturnal itching, linear burrows, erythematous papules in finger webs, wrists, axillae, waist, and genitalia.
indication: First-line topical treatment of Sarcoptes scabiei (scabies) infestation and Pediculus humanus capitis (head lice).
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 13.6 (Scabicides and pediculicides)
safety_note: Apply 5% cream over entire body from neck down to soles of feet. Leave on for 8-14 hours before washing off thoroughly. ALL household members and close sexual contacts must be treated simultaneously. Wash bedding/clothing in hot water.
nlem_reference: NLEM 2022 Section 11.5.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Scabies infestation (Sarcoptes scabiei)
Pediculosis capitis (head lice) and pubic lice

dosage_by_age.children: Infants 2 months–2 years: apply 5% cream to entire body including face, neck, and scalp (avoiding eyes/mouth) under supervision. Leave on for 8–12 hours.
dosage_by_age.adults: 5% cream: apply thoroughly from neck down to soles of feet. Leave on skin for 8–14 hours before washing off. Repeat after 7 days if live mites persist.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Ensure full body coverage including scalp, neck, and behind ears.

max_recommended_dose: One 30g tube usually sufficient for single adult application.
side_effects: Mild transient stinging, burning, itching, erythema (pruritus may persist for 2 weeks after mite eradication)
precautions_contraindications: For external cutaneous use only. Treat all household contacts simultaneously. Wash all bedding and clothing in hot water (>60°C).
clinical_warning: All close household contacts must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection.

symptoms: Conjunctival redness, gritty eye sensation, purulent yellow-green discharge, morning eyelid crusting, tearing.
indication: Topical treatment of acute bacterial conjunctivitis and superficial ocular bacterial infections.
who_reference: Listed in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) - Section 21.1 (Ophthalmic anti-infective medicines)
safety_note: PRESCRIPTION ONLY. Do not wear contact lenses during treatment. Discard bottle 28 days after opening. If severe eye pain, changes in vision, photophobia, or corneal clouding occurs, seek immediate ophthalmologist evaluation.
nlem_reference: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (2025) Section 21.1 • Healthcare Level: P, S, T
common_uses: Acute superficial bacterial conjunctivitis
Bacterial keratitis and external ocular infections

dosage_by_age.children: Eye drops: 1 drop in affected eye(s) every 2–4 hours for children ≥2 years under supervision.
dosage_by_age.adults: Eye drops 0.5%: 1 drop every 2 hours for first 48 hours, then every 4 hours while awake for 5–7 days. Eye ointment 1%: apply at bedtime.
dosage_by_age.elderly: Standard ophthalmic administration.

max_recommended_dose: Ophthalmic formulation; standard course 5 to 7 days.
side_effects: Transient ocular stinging or burning after instillation, local hypersensitivity
precautions_contraindications: For ophthalmic use only. Do not wear contact lenses during treatment. Discontinue if no improvement after 48 hours and consult an ophthalmologist.
clinical_warning: For eye use only. Discontinue and see an eye doctor if vision changes or severe eye pain occurs.
